title: Mind the step
hook: as you watch for nails when walking, watch over your ruling mind (Enchiridion 38)

segments.voice: Yesterday: a role beyond your powers, and the part it pushes aside. Your line was the part that really was yours. Which role did you decline, or wish you had? Day three hundred seventy-three.

Walk barefoot across a garage floor and watch what happens to you. Nobody has to tell you to pay attention. Your eyes go to every step. Your weight hangs back for a beat before each foot lands, just in case there's a nail, a screw, a sharp bit of glass. You do it without thinking, because you know what a nail in the foot feels like. Section thirty-eight of the handbook takes that ordinary carefulness and points it somewhere new. Today: mind the step.
screen: `BAREFOOT ON A GARAGE FLOOR.` → `EVERY STEP WATCHED.` → `MIND THE STEP.`

segments.voice: First, the line. Just as when you walk you take care not to step on a nail or twist your foot, Epictetus says, take care in the same way not to harm your ruling mind. And if we watched for this in every action, we'd go about each one more safely. Second, today's word. The Greek is hēgemonikon, the ruling part. It's related to hēgemōn, a leader or guide. For the Stoics, the hēgemonikon was the command center of a person, the place where impressions are received, judged, and given or refused assent. Chrysippus, one of the school's early heads, even placed it in the heart. Marcus Aurelius uses the word again and again in his private notebook. Third, the nail. Notice how much care we already give the body without effort. We watch for nails, wipe up spills, check the stairs in the dark. Epictetus is asking for the same easy care for the part of us that decides. Fourth, what a nail looks like for the mind. A judgment made in a rush. A resentment you agree to without checking. An impression, he's rude, I'm a failure, it's ruined, accepted at face value. Each one is a small injury to the ruling part, and like a foot injury, it changes how you walk for a while afterward. The fix isn't fear. It's attention at the moment of stepping: a beat before agreeing to the thought, the way you hang back before your foot lands.
screen: `WATCH THE MIND AS YOU WATCH YOUR FEET.` · `HĒGEMONIKON: THE RULING PART.` · `WE ALREADY GUARD THE BODY.` · `A RUSHED JUDGMENT IS A NAIL.` · then, large: `MIND THE STEP.`

segments.voice: If you can stand, stand up and walk, slowly, for the length of the bell. Feel the heel, the ball of the foot, the toes. Let each step be watched, the way you'd cross a floor with nails on it. If you're sitting, rest your feet flat and feel them press the floor. Either way, notice a thought arriving, and give it the same beat you give a step: look before you agree. The bell holds the time.
Hēgemonikon. The Stoic word for the ruling part of the mind, where impressions are judged. Guard it, Epictetus says, as you guard your feet. Today's word.
Your line: a beat before agreeing. Walk carefully for three minutes today, every step watched, and give one hasty thought the same beat. Day three hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism use slow, attentive walking as a reminder to pause before accepting a judgment, guarding the mind as carefully as their footing.

fork.setup: a thought arrives: they ignored my message, so they're angry with me. what does Enchiridion 38 suggest?
options: take the same care as with a nail on the floor: look before you agree.
fork.reveal: guard the ruling mind the way you guard your foot: a beat before you step, or before you agree to the thought.

original.note: Greek: the ruling part, the Stoic word for the mind's command center.

trapdoor: what you thought: watch your step.
what it means: guard the part of you that judges, as carefully as you guard your feet from nails.
what a scholar hears: hēgemonikon, from hēgemōn, a guide; the Stoic command center, which Chrysippus placed in the heart.

sources.ref: Chrysippus on the seat of the hēgemonikon (reported in Galen, On the Doctrines of Hippocrates and Plato)

notes: Enchiridion 38 paraphrased: as in walking you take care not to step on a nail or turn your foot, so take care not to hurt your ruling faculty; if we observe this in every act we shall undertake it more safely. Confirm.
Chrysippus located the hēgemonikon in the heart (Galen, PHP books 2–3). Confirm.
hēgemōn as root and the English 'hegemony': standard etymology; confirm.
Outline practice is a three-minute walk; the in-app sit offers walking if the listener can stand, or feeling the feet if seated.
